title: Why I switched from REST to GraphQL for my last project
excerpt: Lessons learned, what worked, what surprised me, and the gotchas I wish I'd known before flipping the API layer mid-build.

content.text: I had been building a dashboard on a vanilla **REST** stack for about four months when the frontend started growing in ways the backend hadn't anticipated. Every new screen needed half-a-dozen requests, each returning more data than the page actually used. I flipped to **GraphQL** mid-build. Here is what I learned.
What worked immediately
The single-endpoint pattern instantly reduced waterfalls. Pages that used to fire 6-7 sequential requests now made one. Bundle size dropped because we stopped shipping fetch logic for each endpoint.

items: One round-trip per page load — significant on slow networks.
Types generated from the schema gave the frontend free type-safety.
Backend devs and frontend devs spoke the same vocabulary for the first time.

content.text: What surprised me

Caching is harder. REST's URL-as-cache-key falls away — you have to think about Apollo's normalized cache or write resolvers carefully. **N+1 queries** are also easy to introduce: a clean schema can still hammer the database if you skip data-loaders.
GraphQL doesn't make data fetching simpler — it moves where the complexity lives.
content.author: A senior dev I asked midway

content.text: Would I do it again?
Yes, but on **greenfield** projects. Migrating mid-build was expensive — about 3 weeks of friction. If I had started GraphQL on day one, the project would have shipped faster overall.

title: Framer Motion vs. CSS animations — when to reach for which
excerpt: A practical rundown of when each tool shines, plus the performance numbers that actually matter on real devices.

content.text: Both tools are great. They solve different problems. After shipping a few interaction-heavy apps with both, here is the mental model I use.
Reach for CSS when…

items: The animation is **decorative** — hovers, pulses, a button that wobbles.
It doesn't depend on application state.
You want it to keep running even if the JS thread is busy.

content.text: Reach for Framer Motion when…

items: You need to animate based on **state changes** (a modal entering, a list reordering).
You want gesture-driven animations (drag, swipe, pull-to-refresh).
You need orchestration — staggered children, layout transitions, shared elements between routes.

content.text: Performance, honestly

On modern devices both are fine. On older Android phones (Snapdragon 600-class), CSS wins consistently for simple decorative motion — it doesn't fight the React reconciler. For complex orchestrated animations, Framer Motion's optimisations actually outperform what most people write by hand.
Use the smallest tool that solves the problem.
content.author: Every senior engineer ever

title: Notes on shipping faster without breaking everything
excerpt: Small habits that compounded into a much shorter feedback loop — and the temptations to ignore along the way.

content.text: I used to think shipping fast meant typing fast. It does not. It means **shortening the feedback loop** between writing code and knowing whether it works. Here are the small habits that compounded for me.
1. Small commits, small PRs
If a PR takes more than 10 minutes to review, split it. The cost of a long-running branch is not in the code — it's in the rebase pain and the reviewer fatigue.
2. Tests for what you'd regret breaking
Not 100% coverage. Tests for the parts of the system that, if broken silently, would page you at 3am. The rest can wait.
3. Ship behind a flag
Even rough work belongs in main — gated behind a feature flag. It catches **integration issues** weeks earlier than a long-lived branch ever could.
Temptations to ignore

items: Refactoring before you have shipped the feature once.
Adding abstraction for a second use-case that doesn't exist yet.
Bikeshedding the directory structure on day one.

title: Building a real-time chat app with Socket.io
excerpt: A walkthrough of the architecture, the trade-offs I made for presence and message-sync, and how I'd do it differently today.

content.text: Real-time apps look simple until you scale them. Here's how I built a multi-room chat with **presence**, **message history**, and **typing indicators** — and what I'd change today.
Architecture
Node.js + Socket.io on the server, React on the client, **Redis** as the pub/sub layer once we needed more than one server instance. MongoDB stored message history.
The tricky parts

items: Presence — knowing who's online without DDOS-ing the database.
Message ordering when the same user has multiple tabs open.
Reconnection — clients sometimes lose connection without firing 'disconnect'.
Read receipts — surprisingly expensive at scale.

content.text: If I rebuilt it today
I'd start with a hosted service like **Liveblocks** or **PartyKit** for everything except the storage layer. Real-time infra is a deep rabbit hole and the hosted options are good now.

title: TypeScript patterns I use every day
excerpt: A small collection of patterns — utility types, branded types, exhaustive checks — that pay back the type cost many times over.

content.text: TypeScript can feel like overhead until you build the habit of reaching for a handful of patterns. Once they click, they save hours every week.
1. Branded types for IDs
If you have `UserId` and `PostId`, a plain `string` lets you pass them interchangeably. A **branded type** prevents that at compile time with zero runtime cost.

content.code:
type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: 'UserId' }
type PostId = string & { readonly __brand: 'PostId' }

content.text: 2. Exhaustive switch checks
When you add a new variant to a union, you want every relevant switch to break — loudly. The trick: a `never`-typed default case.
3. The unknown type
When you reach for `any`, reach for `unknown` first. It forces you to validate before using — exactly what you want at API boundaries.

title: Why I keep a 'today I learned' log and what it taught me
excerpt: The simple file that improved my engineering more than any course. Two minutes a day, compounding.

content.text: Every day, before I close my laptop, I open a file called **til.md** and write down one thing I learned. Sometimes it's a CLI flag I didn't know about. Sometimes it's a debugging insight that saved me hours. The file is now 3 years old.
Why it works

items: The act of writing forces you to **articulate** what you learned — which exposes the gaps.
Search across years of TILs is a personal Stack Overflow tuned to your own stack.
Reviewing it monthly reveals patterns — am I learning new things, or just stuck on the same problems?

content.text: How to start
Make a single markdown file. Add a date header. Write one bullet. Close it. That's it. Don't over-engineer it — the second you reach for a fancy tool, the habit dies.
An hour of learning a week compounds faster than people think.
content.author: Me, to myself, on hour zero
